shows.title: Upside Down
shows.description:
Alex Israel built his reputation turning the iconography of Los Angeles - sunsets, surfboards, studio-lot backdrops - into slick, self-aware sculpture and painting, and this show distills that project down to a single, obsessively repeated form: the surfboard fin. Four oversized fins, carved from Plexiglas in varying degrees of transparency and gloss, hang upside down from the gallery's ceiling, so that visitors walk beneath them the way a swimmer might glance up at a board passing overhead.

The inversion is the whole idea. Suspended and inverted, the fins nod to the "turtle roll" a surfer performs to punch through a breaking wave, and they turn Gagosian's street-facing Mayfair space into something like an aquarium tank, with passersby on Davies Street peering in at forms that seem to float underwater. Each sculpture takes its title from a well-loved pop song, layering a wash of collective nostalgia over the hard, candy-colored surfaces.

Formally, the work is in dialogue with the Finish Fetish and Light and Space artists who worked in Los Angeles in the 1960s, pairing industrial fabrication with a definite sensuous, almost erotic sheen. But where those artists often kept their materials abstract, Israel's forms stay stubbornly, cheerfully legible as beach culture - more Venice Beach shop window than minimalist tradition, and all the more disarming for it.

It's a tight, single-idea exhibition rather than a sprawling survey, which makes it a good stop for anyone curious about how a artist can wring serious formal ideas out of thoroughly unserious source material. The reflective surfaces also mean the work looks different depending on where you stand and what time of day you visit - worth circling more than once.

shows.title: Emma Reyes
shows.description:
This is the first solo presentation in the UK of Colombian painter Emma Reyes (1919–2003), a self-taught artist whose extraordinary early life — an impoverished Bogotá childhood, a convent upbringing, an escape at eighteen, then encounters across the twentieth century's art world from Diego Rivera's studio to Rome's Futurist circles — reads almost as improbably as her paintings look. Part of White Cube's "Inside the White Cube" series spotlighting artists new to the gallery's roster, the show draws on three series made between 1973 and 1998.

Reyes's work resists easy categorisation: her "Masks" series treats faces as sites of transformation and shifting identity rather than portraiture proper, built from interlocking curvilinear forms in vegetal greens and ochres that recall pre-Columbian ornament and cellular structure in equal measure. Her "Imaginary Portraits," worked entirely from memory with no preparatory drawing, channel the line-work she learned doing embroidery as a convent child into schematic, almost fossil-like figures. A parallel series of fruit and vegetable studies — which she pointedly refused to call still life — blows up the texture of a leaf vein or a tuber's blistered skin until the image outgrows its own frame.

Reyes's own account of her method is worth sitting with: "I do not paint my pictures, I write them." That's a useful way into work built entirely from an internal, non-hierarchical logic where a face and a vegetable receive the same intensity of attention — a genuinely singular painter overdue for wider recognition.

shows.title: Past Presence
shows.description:
A group show built around a simple, rich idea: how contemporary artists reach back through history and make it speak in the present tense. The title borrows from Hiroshi Sugimoto's own Past Presence series, represented here by two blurred, large-format photographs of a Rothko and a Calder — images that lean on the viewer's own visual memory rather than sharp documentary description.

Anish Kapoor's gradated blue-to-cobalt disc picks up the Rothko's chromatic intensity from across the room, while outside the gallery his towering steel Non-Object (Pole) marks a year of major institutional shows for the artist. Elsewhere, Wael Shawky renders a sixteenth-century Persian miniature in Murano glass, Dana Awartani hand-carves a monument to the Temple of Bel (made as Awartani represents Saudi Arabia at the Venice Biennale), and Rodney Graham reworks Cubism through his deadpan "gifted amateur" persona. Masaomi Yasunaga's weathered-looking ceramic vessels and Tunga's cosmetic-mask works on paper close things out with a more unsettled, bodily sense of time passing.

It's a smart, tightly hung survey of Lisson's international roster rather than a single-artist statement, and it rewards attention to the small formal rhymes — a blue here, a grid there — that the hang sets up between wildly different practices and centuries.

shows.title: Lisson Street: Zanzibar
shows.description:
Nine diptychs that Turner Prize-winner Lubaina Himid painted in 1999 are paired here with a 38-minute layered soundtrack composed by her longtime collaborator Magda Stawarska in 2023 — an installation that floats through the gallery on colorful cuboid forms and zigzag patterns rather than hanging flat on the walls. Zanzibar is an outlier in Himid's own account of her work: an almost entirely abstract suite, made in homage to her birthplace, that stands apart from the figurative, storytelling mode she's best known for.

The paintings carry specific, private histories — her father's early death, her mother's grief, half-remembered images of fishing nets, mosquito nets and shuttered windows from a childhood cut short by emigration to England in 1954. Stawarska's sound layer threads Taraab music, opera fragments, archival BBC clips and Himid's own voice through the space, turning the room into something closer to a listening environment than a conventional picture-hang.

It's a rare chance to see this particular chapter of Himid's practice, especially alongside her larger presence this year representing Great Britain at the Venice Biennale — proof that even an artist this exhaustively figurative has, at least once, let a place speak entirely through color and sound.

shows.title: Lisson Street: Pages in situ
shows.description:
A show about Daniel Buren's 8.7cm stripe as it lives on the printed page rather than the gallery wall or the street. Curated by graphic designer Fraser Muggeridge, it gathers more than 100 printed items spanning nearly six decades — magazine interventions, exhibition posters, artist books, invitations — tracing the stripe from an anonymous double-page spread in a 1968 Kunsthalle Düsseldorf catalogue through to a new version of a 1972 Shaftesbury Avenue billboard piece, restaged in cyan for a site in nearby Camden.

For an artist whose signature move is famously "in situ" — made specifically for and inseparable from its site — this is a chance to see how thoroughly that logic extends into ephemera: posters produced with the Antwerp gallery Wide White Space that doubled as artworks and invitations, printed matter that follows the 8.7cm rule without ever showing an actual stripe. The upper gallery also includes striped wall works from 1968 and 1980, applied directly to the architecture.

It's a dense, archival show best suited to close, patient reading rather than a quick walk-through — a portrait of a conceptual artist's six-decade relationship with print culture as much as with painting.

shows.title: Host/Guest
shows.description:
To mark its tenth anniversary, the mental-health arts charity Hospital Rooms takes over Victoria Miro's Wharf Road gallery with a survey of the artworks it has commissioned for NHS mental health wards over the past decade. The show brings together recreations of large-scale new works made this year for hospitals around the country, alongside pieces by artists who have collaborated with the charity since its founding, reflecting on what a decade of embedding original art in NHS mental health environments has actually looked like in practice.

Rather than a conventional gallery survey, Host/Guest functions as a kind of public record of an unusual commissioning model: leading contemporary artists — several of them regulars in Victoria Miro's own program — making work destined not for sale but for wards, corridors and communal rooms where patients live. Seeing that work reassembled in a commercial gallery inverts the charity's usual context and makes visible an initiative that most viewers never otherwise encounter.

The anniversary is being marked with a wider public programme at the gallery, including panel talks, artist workshops and BSL tours, alongside a limited-edition poster series and a benefit auction with Bonhams featuring donated works. It's a short run — under two weeks — timed to close before the charity's wider anniversary events wrap up.

shows.title: Opening Credits
shows.description:
John Currin's new body of work sets pairs and trios of exaggeratedly built women into ornamental, Arcadian landscapes, borrowing the poses and self-conscious display of 1970s clothing-catalogue models and running them through the machinery of classical figure painting. Twelve mid-size canvases are joined by a group of ink drawings on washed paper that restate the same poses in a sparer, more graphic register, plus preparatory sketches shown alongside the finished works.

Currin, who opened this gallery's very first show back in 1997, is working in familiar territory — the tension between academic virtuosity and frank, often comic sexuality — but pushes his figures further into caricature and age here, with bodies that slip between the idealized and the fantastic. The landscapes borrow explicitly from Poussin and Watteau's Cythera while grounding themselves in the real topography of Acadia National Park in Maine, a pun on "Arcadia" that runs through the whole show.

It's a mature, funny, technically dazzling exhibition from an artist who has spent three decades making the collision of high painterly craft and lowbrow fantasy his signature move, and this show finds him aging his own cast of characters right along with himself.

shows.title: This Weather
shows.description:
Helen Marten, best known for dense, materially inventive sculpture, presents a five-chapter film here — a restaging of a work originally conceived as part of her opera 30 Blizzards., commissioned by Miu Miu for Art Basel Paris in 2025. Each chapter is voiced by a different female monologue tied to a symbolic life-stage — childhood, community, sexuality, interiority, loss — spoken by archetypal figures like the mother, the child, the patient, the widow and the lover, though Marten treats these as ciphers for metaphor rather than literal characters.

The five monologues, performed by actors including Kathryn Hunter and Sophia Al-Maria, are set against animation by Adam Sinclair and a score by Beatrice Dillon, building what Marten calls a "molecular" universe where weather, material conditions, and psychological states all sit on the same plane. It's a natural extension of her sculptural practice's interest in categorization and strange taxonomies, just translated into moving image and language.

Marten — a Turner Prize and Hepworth Prize winner who has increasingly folded writing and now performance into her work — uses the film to think through how identity fragments into a system of interlocking, planet-like states of mind. It's a demanding, literary piece best experienced start to finish, and a good example of how far her practice has moved beyond the object since her breakthrough a decade ago.

shows.title: Backyard Biennial: East
shows.description:
Whitechapel Gallery's 125th-anniversary summer takes the form of an eight-week, free festival spread across more than forty partner venues throughout East London — galleries, synagogues, community centres, artist studios, a former hospital, even the Tower of London — rather than a single exhibition behind one set of doors. Inside the gallery itself, the biennial threads together several strands: the group show East of the Aldgate Pump, a participatory rope-making installation called The Ropery made with designer Sanne Visser, a summer residency and craft programme by the Bengali arts organisation OITIJ-JO Collective, Fozia Ismail's interactive installation around the endangered Somali wedding basket, and daily film programming built around East End filmmaker John Smith and community archives.

What makes it worth tracking as its own entry is the sheer scale of collaboration: participating organisations range from Raven Row and Public Gallery to the Jewish Museum London, Bevis Marks Synagogue, Auto Italia and dozens of grassroots groups, each staging their own strand of programming under the biennial's loose curatorial umbrella of migration, land, craft and community memory. It's less a conventional biennial than an attempt to redefine what one can be — built from the ground up with the neighbourhood's own cultural infrastructure rather than imported curatorial concepts.

As the pilot edition of what Whitechapel intends as a recurring project, Backyard Biennial: East doubles as a survey of the East End's current community-arts ecosystem, timed to close on the same day as a citywide finale procession and performance at the Tower of London.

shows.title: East of the Aldgate Pump
shows.description:
Named for the historic water pump that once marked the informal boundary between the City of London and the East End, this group show gathers twelve artists across three galleries to think through the crossings — social, cultural, geographic — that have defined East London for centuries. It's organized in three loose movements: migration and journeying, explored partly through patchwork as both material technique and metaphor; the intimacies and frictions of city life and kinship; and food's role in tying together heritage, migration and the seasonal rhythms of community.

The artist list is deliberately cross-generational and international, pairing East End veterans like Denzil Forrester — whose paintings have long channeled the energy of London's reggae and dub sound-system culture — with younger or newer voices such as Nour Jaouda, whose dyed textile works draw on prayer-mat forms, and Rene Matić, working across photography and installation to probe belonging and resistance. Jyll Bradley's photographic self-portraits from her archive sit alongside Reetu Sattar's film and installation work and a collaborative sound/perfume piece by Adam Farah-Saad and Ezra Lloyd Jackson.

The show anchors Whitechapel Gallery's own contribution to Backyard Biennial, the gallery's inaugural East End-wide festival marking its 125th anniversary, and functions as a kind of core sample of a neighborhood whose creative identity the gallery has been entangled with since 1901.

shows.title: Like Music in the Blood
shows.artist: Benjamin Orlow, Emil Sands, Galli, Hannah Quinlan and Rosie Hastings, Kira Freije, Suleman Aqeel Khilji, Tanoa Sasraku, Tiona Nekkia McClodden
shows.description:
This eight-artist group show takes the body as its subject, but almost never head-on — each artist here approaches selfhood through a kind of formal indirection, whether that's omission, disfigurement, projection or metaphor. The title's simile is the key: these are artists who describe embodiment "like" something else, understanding that representation is always an approximation rather than a transcription.

The range of material is wide. Suleman Aqeel Khilji builds hazy, sepia-toned paintings from distemper and pigment washes that read like excavated memories of his native Quetta; Galli's silhouetted figures, made since the late 1970s Berlin scene, stage myth and metamorphosis with a stark economy of line; Benjamin Orlow's monumental clay, plaster and bronze figures — suspended on scaffolds and slings — teeter between the heroic and the collapsing. Tanoa Sasraku (Turner Prize shortlisted for 2026) sun-bleaches and clips newspaper into torso-shaped relics, while Kira Freije casts hands and faces from friends and family onto stainless-steel armatures for an immersive sculptural tableau. Hannah Quinlan and Rosie Hastings work in fresco to restage the politics of queer visibility within Britain's built environment, and Tiona Nekkia McClodden's leatherwork — scarred, shoe-polished, bound in kinbaku rope — draws on BDSM practice as a study of power, care and duress.

It's a demanding, sensorially rich show, less interested in a single thesis about "the body" than in demonstrating how many different sculptural and painterly vocabularies can be bent toward the same impossible task: picturing an interior life from the outside.

shows.title: She Flickered In and Out of History
shows.description:
Elisa Giardina Papa's video and mixed-media installation takes as its subject a genuinely strange episode of geological and political history: in 1831, an underwater volcanic eruption briefly raised a new island between Sicily and Tunisia, triggering a sovereignty dispute among European powers before the island sank back beneath the waves six months later. Giardina Papa uses this footnote — an island that appeared, was fought over, and then refused to be claimed by anyone — as a way into questions of Mediterranean history, colonialism and queer and decolonial temporality.

The work itself was filmed on Mount Etna, Stromboli and the submerged slopes of the volcanic islands, and is presented on a large freestanding LED screen alongside sculptures made from hand-shaped glass and cotisso, the raw, unstable glass usually destined for remelting in Murano's furnaces. A poem spoken in Sicilian, set to a score by composer duendita, threads through the video, weaving archival research into something more speculative and lyrical; the glass sculptures, meanwhile, draw their deep, shifting colours from historical accounts of the strangely tinted skies that followed the 1831 eruption.

This is the third in a trilogy of video works by Giardina Papa exploring forgotten Mediterranean histories, following U Scantu, which premiered at the Venice Biennale in 2022 — and it continues her sustained interest in forms of knowledge that official histories have discarded or never recorded to begin with.

shows.title: Still Life
shows.description:
Jasper Marsalis's first UK institutional exhibition turns Chisenhale's gallery into something between a screening room and a surveillance hub. A huge cinematic screen cycles through live feeds pulled from unsecured internet-connected cameras trained on landscapes around the world — lakes, hills, a chicken coop, streetlights tracing roads at night — each view held for roughly thirty seconds before switching to the next. Four hanging speakers pull in live FM radio signals and turn them into a low, droning wash of sound that hangs over the space.

Marsalis, a London-based artist and musician, is using found, unauthored material rather than material he's shot or composed himself; an algorithm decides which camera feed plays when, so the installation is always slightly different depending on when you catch it. The effect recalls the contemplative function of historic landscape painting, except the "landscape" here is contingent on whatever some remote, forgotten webcam happens to be broadcasting at that moment — a meditation on how thoroughly networks of surveillance and transmission have replaced older, slower ways of looking at the world.

It's a spare, atmospheric show, more environment than object-based exhibition, and one of the more unusual entries in Chisenhale's long run of first-UK-show commissions for early-career artists.

shows.title: Small Sculptures of the 1970s
shows.description:
This is Richard Tuttle's seventh show with Modern Art, and it goes back to a specific, little-seen chapter of his history: hand-sized assemblages he made in New York in the early-to-mid 1970s, near the end of a stretch in which his work moved sharply toward material and formal reduction. Much of it hasn't been shown publicly in decades.

The works are modest in scale but not in ambition — lengths of painted wire tracing a volume of space, jigsaw-cut plywood and timber slats that collapse and rebuild spatial relationships within a few inches of material. They arrived at a moment when American Minimalism was trending toward big, fabricated, industrial objects, and Tuttle went the opposite way, prioritizing the overlooked and the structurally vulnerable — pieces that, in his own words, "vanish" rather than last. The show also includes Homage to Claude (1977), first shown at that year's Whitney Biennial.

Seeing this body of work now, decades after the controversy it caused at the Whitney in 1975 (a show that indirectly led to the founding of the New Museum), is a chance to watch a major artist's minimal vocabulary take shape in real time — small, quiet, and still oddly radical.

shows.title: Variation
shows.artist: Pablo Bronstein, Mathew Cerletty, Matt Connors, Cary Kwok, Lucia Di Luciano, Christina Mackie, Joan Nelson, Amalia Pica, Amedeo Polazzo, Nicole Wermers
shows.description:
A tight group show that reads like a cross-section of the gallery's range: ten artists, ten very different ideas of what a picture or an object can do. Nicole Wermers contributes a deadpan sculptural gag - a handsewn faux-fur "tail" on a hose reel that can stretch ten metres across the room - while Pablo Bronstein's finely inked architectural fantasy imagines a clock built to a synthetic sapphire's scale. Painting carries much of the rest of the show: Mathew Cerletty's spare, uncanny realism, Christina Mackie's loose oil studies, Joan Nelson's glittered, crayon-dark landscape, and Amedeo Polazzo's saturated abstraction sit alongside the geometric rigor of Lucia Di Luciano, an Italian op-art veteran whose inclusion gives the show some historical ballast.

Matt Connors' coloured-pencil work and Cary Kwok's meticulously inked, framed drawing add a more intimate, graphic register, while Amalia Pica's watercolour-and-pencil "Daisy Chain" continues her long interest in modest materials standing in for social connection. Taken together, "Variation" doesn't argue a thesis so much as demonstrate a house style built from divergence - each artist pursuing an entirely private logic, hung close enough to spark unexpected conversations between them.

The show is at Herald St's Bloomsbury outpost on Museum Street, one of the gallery's three current London and Bologna spaces.

shows.title: Quentin James McCaffrey
shows.description:
Quentin James McCaffrey's first UK solo show gathers a suite of small, meticulously painted interiors that read like stills from a film no one has seen. The New York-based painter builds his rooms from imagination rather than observation, splicing architectural details from different eras into settings that feel plausible but slightly unmoored in time. Mirrors, potted plants, draped fabric, and framed pictures stand in for human presence, doing the emotional work that figures would normally carry.

Compared to McCaffrey's earlier, more cluttered compositions, the paintings here are pared back, letting empty space and directional light take the lead. Sunbeams cut across floors and bounce off mirrored surfaces, creating quiet double exposures of interior and exterior, or of one moment layered on another. The compositions owe a visible debt to Quattrocento perspective and Dutch Golden Age domestic scenes, but McCaffrey uses those historical structures as scaffolding rather than subject matter, aiming for atmosphere over citation.

The centerpiece, an eleven-panel work titled The True Veil, extends this fragmented, mirror-and-doorway logic across a grid of small canvases, turning a single imagined room into a sequence of partial views. It's a good demonstration of what makes these paintings rewarding up close: their scale is intimate, but the spatial games are anything but simple, and they ask for the kind of slow looking that rushed gallery visits rarely allow.

shows.title: One Table, Two Chairs (一桌二椅)
shows.description:
Xue Ruozhe's first show with MASSIMODECARLO's London space takes its title and its logic from Chinese opera, where a single table and two chairs can stand in for a palace or a battlefield and the audience fills in the rest. The paintings here work on the same principle of extreme reduction: restrained, largely tonal compositions built from warm greys, blacks and the barest suggestion of color, following the classical ink-painting idea of liu bai, or "leaving blank," where empty space is treated as active rather than absent.

Across the three rooms, pairs of girls recur — crossing a river, catching their own reflections, turning to face what turns out to be themselves. Xue, who trained at China's Central Academy of Fine Arts and later at the Royal College of Art in London, has described each painting as a kind of self-portrait staged through these figures, with a submerged retelling of the Perseus myth (recast with a female protagonist, and without Medusa ever appearing) running underneath the surface.

It's a quiet, exacting body of work — paintings that ask you to slow down and notice how much is being withheld, and how much that withholding is doing.

shows.title: Summer Show
shows.description:
Goodman Gallery's annual summer group show is less a themed exhibition than a chance to see the roster's range side by side — new and historical work by Ghada Amer, William Kentridge, David Koloane, Laura Lima, Misheck Masamvu, Cassi Namoda, Georgina Maxim, Pamela Phatsimo Sunstrum and Yinka Shonibare, hung so that formal and material affinities surface without being forced into a single argument.

Kentridge's bronze sculpture Washer, part of his ongoing series of elemental glyph-figures, greets visitors alongside Yinka Shonibare's textile piece African Flower Magic, which depicts endangered flora native to the arid regions of South Africa's Northern Cape and Namibia — an apt pairing of two artists who both use process-heavy, craft-inflected media to carry political weight. Elsewhere, Cassi Namoda's warm, narrative figuration sits against David Koloane's expressionist Johannesburg-era abstraction, and Ghada Amer's stitched and appliquéd canvases bring a different register of embroidery-as-subversion into the mix.

It's a useful primer on a gallery whose program has, since apartheid-era South Africa, consistently centered African and diasporic artists engaging with postcolonial history — several of the artists here are concurrently on view in major European survey shows, from the Barbican's Panafrica exhibition to a group show in Seville, underscoring how live this material currently is on the international circuit.

shows.title: Richard Pettibone
shows.description:
Richard Pettibone (1938–2024) spent six decades making meticulously rendered, drastically shrunk-down copies of other artists' most iconic works, and this is the first UK solo show devoted to his singular brand of appropriation. Organised with the Pettibone Estate and Castelli Gallery — which began showing him in 1969 — the exhibition spans paintings from 1967 to 2021, tracking a practice built almost entirely on translation, miniaturisation and repetition.

The reference points are art-historical blue chips: Warhol's Campbell's Soup Cans and Flowers, Lichtenstein's comic-panel women, Duchamp's Fountain, Jasper Johns' flags, Frank Stella's shaped canvases. Pettibone doesn't merely reproduce these images; executed at a fraction of their original scale, each small painting becomes an act of close, almost devotional looking, turning appropriation into something more intimate than critique — closer to collecting, or to memory.

Seen fifty years on, in a moment saturated with image circulation and remix culture, Pettibone's obsessive small-scale homages feel less like a Pop-era footnote and more like an early, prescient meditation on how images accrue meaning through repetition and reduced scale — a theme this compact but rich exhibition traces from the mid-1960s all the way to the artist's late work.

shows.title: Nomenclature for the Time Being
shows.artist: Rebecca Bellantoni, Hannah Black, Maren Hassinger, Deborah-Joyce Holman, Marla-Sunshine Kellard-Jones, Atiéna R. Kilfa, Christine Kirubi, Kumbirai Makumbe, Zanele Muholi, Sandra Mujinga, Shenece Oretha, Ingrid Pollard, Ebun Sodipo
shows.dates_note: Raven Row's own site (ravenrow.org) is JavaScript-only and returned no readable content even after repeated fetch attempts; dates given here (21 May-6 Sep 2026) are corroborated consistently across multiple independent listings (GalleriesNow, Heni, e-flux, ArtFacts) and the show is also named as Raven Row's contribution to Whitechapel Gallery's Backyard Biennial, which the Whitechapel site confirms runs through 6 Sep 2026.
shows.description:
Curated by Imani Mason Jordan with research by Nikita Sena Quarshie, this group exhibition gathers thirteen artists working primarily in sculpture — alongside performance, writing, photography and video — to propose that shared political and social conditions can produce shared material instincts. The premise, in the curator's phrase, is a kind of Black feminist materiality: objects treated not as inert things but as social and political actors in their own right.

The artist list spans generations and geographies, from Maren Hassinger and Zanele Muholi to younger practitioners like Sandra Mujinga, Deborah-Joyce Holman and Ebun Sodipo, allowing the show to trace continuities in how Black and queer artists have used sculptural form — rope, wire, leather, wax, concrete, glass — to hold difficult histories without simply illustrating them. Ingrid Pollard and Christine Kirubi's work extends the show's material concerns into landscape and place, while performance and writing components (from Rebecca Bellantoni and others) keep the exhibition from settling into static display.

Staged in Raven Row's converted eighteenth-century Spitalfields townhouses, the show benefits from a setting whose own layered history of migration and craft — Huguenot silk weavers, and generations of new Londoners since — quietly echoes the exhibition's concerns with material inheritance. It is also Raven Row's contribution to the inaugural Whitechapel Gallery Backyard Biennial, timed to the gallery's 125th anniversary summer of East End-wide programming.

shows.title: The Nabi Shock
shows.description:
Waddington Custot pairs more than twenty paintings by the Nabis — Bonnard, Vuillard, Maurice Denis, Paul Sérusier, Émile Bernard, Ker-Xavier Roussel and others, all made in the extraordinarily compressed twelve years between 1888 and 1900 — with new work by a group of contemporary painters including Marcel.la Barceló, Ian Davenport, Marcel Dzama, Anne Rothenstein and Fabienne Verdier. The premise is a direct formal lineage: the Nabis' insistence, per Denis's famous dictum, that a painting is "essentially a flat surface covered with colours" before it's anything else, and the way that flatness, pattern and interiority still show up in studio practices today.

The historical half of the show favours intimate, domestic subjects — sisters, wives, quiet interiors, secluded gardens — rendered in the group's characteristic unmodulated colour fields and tactile surfaces, alongside more unexpected inclusions like Maurice Denis's stained-glass design for Le Cheval blanc and Bonnard's illustrated concert programmes. The contemporary pairing isn't subtle about its throughlines: Davenport's poured-colour panels sit against Filiger's chromatic studies, Verdier's ink-and-acrylic abstractions extend Vuillard's dialogue between interior and exterior experience, and Rothenstein's sunset panels nod to Vallotton's nocturnal landscapes.

It's a smart piece of programming for a gallery on Cork Street with real expertise in this period, less a straightforward survey than an argument for the Nabis' continued relevance to painters working in figuration and pattern today.

shows.title: something old, something new, something borrowed, something blue
shows.description:
Autumn Wallace's second solo show with Josh Lilley takes its title from the old wedding rhyme, but turns its promise of good luck inside out into a meditation on grief and inheritance. The Philadelphia-born artist works in sculpture and painting, building figures and hybrid creatures out of leather, textile, and found material that carry the visible history of their own making — creased skins, sewn-over seams, stretched hides that read like scar tissue.

Recurring characters such as Brer Bear appear throughout the exhibition as stand-ins for the push and pull of care and dependency, love shading into obligation. Wallace treats her materials as collaborators rather than raw stock: mosaic-like surfaces built from repurposed textile sit alongside bodies studded with gems and found ornament, so that ideas of protection, wound, and adornment blur into one another.

A text by poet Roya Marsh accompanies the show, underscoring its interest in what gets passed down between generations — objects, gestures, rituals — and how mourning reshapes those inheritances rather than simply ending them. It's a strong, tactile body of work from an artist still early in her career but clearly building a distinct visual language around loss, survival, and the afterlife of materials.

shows.title: Interactionship
shows.description:
Agata Bogacka's second show with Edel Assanti is built from a tight, controlled vocabulary of gradients, voids and near-touching planes of colour. The Polish painter uses fluid, thinly worked paint alongside passages of bare, untouched canvas, and the friction between the two — saturated colour fading into raw surface — becomes her way of picturing negotiation, conflict and the uneven distribution of power.

The paintings don't illustrate politics directly, but they're made in direct response to the volatile political climate in Bogacka's native Poland and beyond. Shapes are kept deliberately apart or allowed to meet only briefly at their edges, their borders blurred by shifts in density and tone rather than hard lines — a formal strategy that stands in for the instability, inequality and dependency she sees structuring relationships at every scale, from the personal to the geopolitical.

It's a spare, exacting body of work: abstraction used not to escape the world's pressures but to distill them, canvas by canvas, into a private, tense visual language.

shows.title: Abstract Pairings
shows.description:
A tightly structured survey of British abstraction, this show pairs two works apiece by six artists — Bernard Cohen, Liza Giles, Michael Kidner, Tom Phillips, Carol Robertson and Richard Smith — so that each artist's own development becomes a miniature conversation within the larger one. It's a smart curatorial device: rather than a chronological sweep, the hang invites direct comparison between, say, an early and a late Michael Kidner, or Bernard Cohen's 1970s cluster paintings against a work made two decades later.

The generational range is wide. Kidner, a pioneer of British Op Art, moves from 1950s Rothko-inflected colour fields to chaos-theory-driven geometry in the 1990s. Richard Smith's shaped, sculptural canvas and related work on paper recall his stint representing Britain at the 1970 Venice Biennale, while Tom Phillips' dense, calligraphic abstractions nod to Rilke and to his own decades-long Humument project. Liza Giles is the outlier and the youngest voice here, her raw-canvas, cut-and-reassembled panels drawing on London's skyline in blues and greens.

Seen together, the works make a quiet case for abstraction as a continuous, still-evolving British tradition rather than a fixed mid-century moment — useful counter-programming to the market's usual focus on a handful of canonical names.

shows.title: Alphabets
shows.description:
Ali Kazim's first solo show with Cristea Roberts brings together watercolours and his debut suite of prints, a portfolio of nineteen etchings and aquatints each keyed to a letter of the Urdu alphabet. Trained partly in the tradition of South Asian miniature painting, Kazim uses the alphabet primer format — the qaida that generations of Pakistani and Indian schoolchildren have learned from — as a scaffold for meditations on migration, language loss, and the layered, often violent history of the subcontinent.

The prints move between the intimate and the historical: a tiger leaping through a flaming circus hoop sits alongside Tipu's Tiger, the eighteenth-century automaton now in the V&A that depicts a British soldier being mauled, and Koh-i-Noor, a spectral outline of the diamond seized into the Crown Jewels. Elsewhere Kazim finds equal weight in everyday things — a washing line, a shattered tea set, a hoopoe bird drawn from Sufi poetry — rendered with the same patient, layered watercolour technique the artist has spent years refining.

The exhibition also marks the UK launch of Kazim's book Alphabet Book | Urdu Qaida, made with curator Hammad Nasar, and coincides with his inclusion in a group show on land and material at Drawing Room later in September. For anyone interested in how printmaking can carry the weight of oral and written language traditions, this is a rare chance to see a full alphabet-driven suite in one room.

shows.title: A Primer of Birds
shows.description:
Taking its title from a rare 1970s poetry collaboration between Ted Hughes and Leonard Baskin, this group show gathers more than 25 works by artists who have used birds as a way of thinking about character, mortality, and the natural world. It's a survey exhibition in the best sense — a chance to see how differently painters and printmakers across generations have handled the same basic motif.

Georg Baselitz's eagles, a recurring subject in his graphic work since the 1970s, read as self-portraits in disguise, while Paula Rego's crows and "bird women" carry the weight of grief and superstition in equal measure — three works made in the years following her husband's death. Julian Opie contributes a deadpan series of Australian urban birds, Yinka Shonibare pairs endangered African species with ritual masks, and Fernand Léger's 1955 lithograph of a Parisian bird-seller nods to the parrots once stationed atop the Eiffel Tower as an early-warning system. Hew Locke, Jim Dine, Mimmo Paladino, Joe Tilson and Tom Hammick round out the roster.

Taken together the prints and works on paper suggest less a themed group show than a loose anthology — each artist arriving at birds from a completely different direction, whether ecological, autobiographical, or purely formal, and the accumulation is what makes the show worth lingering over.

shows.title: Sensual / Mutual
shows.description:
This is the first major UK institutional solo show for Del LaGrace Volcano, the photographer whose work has shaped queer and trans visual culture since the 1970s. Rather than revisit the artist's best-known staged and studio portraiture, the exhibition pulls unseen material from the archive: pictures made in San Francisco's Scott's P.I.T. leather dyke bar, the rent-striking Goodman Building hotel, and ARF, a women's land commune in the mountains above Santa Fe. Together they trace a specific, undernarrated geography of 1970s-80s queer and feminist life.

What comes through in the prints on view is less the confrontational eroticism Volcano is often filed under and more an intimate, documentary tenderness — portraits of friends, lovers and collaborators who were, crucially, not passive subjects but participants in a shared political project. The images sit at the intersection of activism and art-making, produced from within the communities they depict rather than at a remove from them.

Seeing this work now, amid new waves of anti-trans legislation and the disappearance of queer nightlife spaces in London and elsewhere, gives the show an unmistakable present-tense urgency; it isn't presented as nostalgia but as a working archive of how queer collective life gets built, and rebuilt, under pressure. It's a rare chance to see this depth of Volcano's early practice outside of a university archive.

shows.title: Death's Sacred Mirror
shows.description:
Thomas Houseago has turned the gallery into something between a cabinet of curiosities and a private reliquary, curating his own new sculptures alongside a startling range of borrowed and ancient objects — Egyptian, Greek and Aztec artifacts sit near works by Louise Bourgeois, Joseph Beuys, Lucio Fontana, Meret Oppenheim and Henri Matisse. The premise, borrowed from the obsidian "smoking mirrors" of Aztec ritual, treats the show itself as a kind of divinatory surface: a way of seeing Houseago's own towering, visceral figures reflected back through millennia of sculptural history.

At the center is a new edition of Houseago's Crystal No. 1, a patinated brass form that marks a shift in the artist's usual vocabulary of hulking, masculine figures toward something more crystalline and interior. Smaller bronzes and plaster works — Swan, Small Standing Figure, Cosmic Egg — read almost like votive objects when set against the antiquities Houseago has chosen as their neighbors, on loan from London dealers Rupert Wace and Charles Ede.

What makes the exhibition distinctive is the curatorial hand of the artist himself: rather than a survey of his own practice, it's a staged conversation across time, in which a Cycladic idol, a Beuys vitrine and a Houseago totem are all made to argue the same case about what sculpture is for. It rewards slow looking — this is a show built for wandering rather than a quick lap of the room.

shows.title: Playing the Piano Upstairs
shows.description:
Sayuri Ichida's exhibition is built around handmade, luminous prints made in the snow-bound landscapes of rural Japan, where the artist has been working through memory, grief and the bond between sisters. The photographs favor stark, high-contrast black-and-white tonality — figures standing in still water, silhouettes against white snowfields, a body wrapped in reeds — that gives the work an almost ritual, out-of-time quality.

Ichida's printing technique is as much the subject as the imagery: her prints are worked by hand in ways that emphasize texture and light, turning photographic paper into something closer to a drawn or painted surface. That handcraft matches the show's themes of loss and remembrance, treating the photographic print itself as a vessel for feeling rather than simple documentation.

It's an intimate, quietly intense body of work, suited to the Photographers' Gallery's smaller upstairs spaces, and a good introduction to an artist still building an international reputation.

shows.title: Japanese Women Photographers: From 1950s to Now
shows.description:
This survey brings together 27 women photographers working in Japan from the 1950s to the present, reframing a history of Japanese photography that has traditionally centered a handful of male names. The show ranges from postwar documentary photographers capturing hospitals and street life through to contemporary artists like Rinko Kawauchi and Mika Ninagawa, whose color-saturated, sensorial images of eyes, flowers and fish sit at the other end of the medium's possibilities.

Along the way it takes in intimate, sometimes confrontational body-focused work — nude self-portraiture during pregnancy, close studies of skin and touch — alongside quieter landscape and still-life photography, such as views of Mount Fuji rendered as a hazy, near-abstract presence. The through-line is less a single style than a shared insistence on photographing lived, embodied experience from a woman's vantage point, across seven decades of dramatic change in Japanese society.

For a gallery devoted to expanding photography's canon, this is an ambitious, long-overdue rebalancing act, and the sheer range of approaches on view — from gritty black-and-white documentary to hyper-color pop imagery — makes it a rich show to spend real time with.

shows.title: Captive Blooms
shows.description:
Mika Ninagawa's large-scale photographs take over the Soho Photography Quarter's outdoor display windows with her signature hyper-saturated color work: schools of ornamental goldfish glowing under tanks of red and blue light, and cherry blossoms shot in almost fluorescent close-up pink. Ninagawa has built a career on maximalist color and sugar-bright artifice, treating nature — fish, flowers — as ready-made spectacle rather than something to be observed quietly.

Shown as a free, walk-up outdoor exhibition rather than inside the gallery, the work functions almost like a public art commission, turning a stretch of Soho street into a glowing, immersive install. It's an accessible entry point into Ninagawa's practice for passers-by who might never step into a gallery, and a striking use of the Photographers' Gallery's public-facing Soho Photography Quarter site.

Given the long run — over a year — this is very much part of the neighborhood's fabric for now, worth a look any time you're passing through Soho.

shows.title: Some Distance Apart
shows.description:
Jonathan Wateridge's third show with GRIMM, and his second at the gallery's London space, gathers new oil paintings that treat the human figure the way classical tragedy treats fate — as something suspended, inevitable, and about to happen. Bodies tumble and collide mid-motion in seascapes and interiors rendered with a cinematic sense of framing, their gestures frozen at the exact moment before consequence lands.

Wateridge, who trained partly through film before turning to painting, keeps returning to thresholds: a face bisected by a hard line in Siren (borrowed from a still of Dominique Sanda in Bertolucci's The Conformist), a solitary red figure clutching a mask in Persona, two figures calling out toward the viewer in Signal. The paintings favour saturated, theatrical colour — vermilion, black, blanched white — over naturalism, and the effect is less narrative illustration than mood held at a rolling boil.

The show's title captures its central preoccupation: figures that read as simultaneously near and far, legible and dissolving, caught in what Wateridge treats as an extended moment of anticipation rather than a resolved scene. It's a good entry point for anyone curious about how contemporary figurative painting can borrow the structure of classical myth without illustrating it literally.
shows.reception: Thursday, 8 October 2026, 6:30pm (artist in conversation with Lydia Figes for the launch of the monograph "Diorama")

shows.title: The Northeast Corridor
shows.artist: Katherine Bradford, Joe Bradley, Kathy Butterly, Lois Dodd, Nicole Eisenman, Allison Gildersleeve, Mala Iqbal, Alex Katz, Roberto Lugo, Lisa Sanditz, Peter Saul, Dasha Shishkin, Judith Simonian, Simi Stone, Daniel Um, Peter Williams
shows.description:
Co-curated with participating artist Lisa Sanditz, The Northeast Corridor takes its structure from a piece of American infrastructure — the Amtrak rail line linking Washington D.C. to Boston — and uses it to loosely map a constellation of painters and sculptors whose lives and studios sit along that route. It's a smart curatorial device: rather than grouping artists by style or generation, the show groups them by geography and the informal networks of community that geography produces.

The range on view is wide by design. Alex Katz's flat, elegant figuration and Lois Dodd's plein-air-inflected landscape painting sit alongside Peter Saul's cartoonish, confrontational satire and Nicole Eisenman's loose, expressive watercolours; Kathy Butterly's glazed, bodily ceramics and Roberto Lugo's ornately painted stoneware bring sculpture into a conversation otherwise dominated by paint. Younger and mid-career voices like Katherine Bradford, Allison Gildersleeve, Mala Iqbal and Daniel Um sit comfortably alongside the more established names, which is really the point — the show argues for a shared regional sensibility that cuts across age and reputation.

Spread across both of the gallery's Mayfair spaces, it's an unusually generous survey of contemporary American painting for a commercial London gallery, with real crowd-pleasers (Katz, Saul, Eisenman) alongside artists who deserve wider attention here.

shows.title: The suspense is terrible, I hope it will last
shows.description:
Andrea Ferrero's London solo debut takes the shrunken, plasticky world of childhood toys and blows it up to the scale of urban infrastructure. Working from her residency at the Delfina Foundation, the Lima-born artist has translated decorative details lifted from London's gates, railings and garden enclosures — the ornamental hardware of the city's architectures of security — into oversized padlocks styled after Polly Pocket sets and Little Tikes playhouses.

The joke, and the argument, is that these objects sit uneasily between collectible toy and actual security device: candy-coloured surfaces standing in for the mechanisms that quietly police who gets access to which parts of a city. Ferrero has spent her practice tracing how systems of power and ownership get rehearsed in miniature, through playscapes, dollhouses and imagined banquets, and this show pushes that idea specifically into London's street furniture and boundary markers.

It's a tightly focused, single-idea exhibition rather than a survey, which suits Ferrero's sculptural approach — better to see one argument followed all the way through than watered down across many. Worth catching for anyone interested in how domestic-scale objects can carry outsized political weight.

shows.title: Interweave
shows.description:
Interweave brings together five artists — Bea Bonafini, Adam de Boer, LoVid, Joan Truckenbrod and aurèce vettier — for whom textile processes are a way of thinking rather than just a technique. Batik, tapestry, Jacquard weaving, carpet inlay and embroidery sit alongside video, AI-generated imagery and other computational tools, and the show's premise is that these seemingly opposed traditions — ancient hand-craft and emerging technology — actually share a logic: both build meaning through accumulation, repetition and layering.

Bea Bonafini's carpet-inlay works translate painterly gesture into cut and pieced textile, while Adam de Boer folds batik technique (learned through his Indonesian heritage) into scenes of contemporary Los Angeles. LoVid, the duo behind several of the show's more overtly technological pieces, and Joan Truckenbrod, a pioneer of computer-generated textile-adjacent imagery since the 1970s, both treat the loom and the algorithm as parallel systems for generating pattern. aurèce vettier's contributions lean toward the uncanny and hallucinatory, populated by half-glimpsed spectral figures.

It's a smart, tightly curated survey of how craft-based making has migrated into contemporary practice without losing its handmade texture — worth seeing for anyone interested in where textile art currently sits between traditional making and digital production.

shows.title: Learning to Fly
shows.description:
Eileen Cooper has spent five decades painting a single recurring figure - a large, physically emphatic woman who stands in for autobiography, myth and fairy tale all at once - and this new body of work pushes that figure into the studio itself. In "Red Studio with Peonies" and "Side On," the artist's usual outdoor settings give way to interiors so saturated with red that they feel less like rooms than states of mind: womb-like enclosures where a woman at work on a self-portrait catches a different face in the mirror than the one she's painting.

Water and wind run through the show as a kind of undertow. Shawls spill like liquid across tabletops, rugs float on seas of turbulent brushwork, and in the title painting a woman drops or is lifted through open sky, arms and legs caught mid-current above rolling hills and skeletal, just-budding trees. Cooper keeps her scenes deliberately open-ended, but the recurring plunges and immersions read as a meditation on instability - creative and otherwise - met without panic.

It's a good showcase of what makes Cooper, a former Royal Academy Keeper, distinctive: figuration that borrows the charge of myth without illustrating it literally, and a colour sense (those insistent reds and blues) that does as much emotional work as the imagery itself.

shows.title: Rumours
shows.description:
To mark its fifteenth anniversary, Large Glass has pulled together a group show drawing on work by roughly two dozen artists who have passed through its program since 2011, selected from more than fifty exhibitions. Rather than organizing the show around a theme, the gallery has built it around its own history — pairing pieces by photographers like Guido Guidi, John Gossage, Mark Ruwedel and Gerry Johansson with sculpture and object-based work by artists such as Tonico Lemos Auad, Martino Gamper, Richard Wentworth, Cerith Wyn Evans and Hendl Helen Mirra.

The title nods to the Fleetwood Mac album, and the exhibition leans into that spirit of things half-remembered and reshuffled: photographs of landscape and architecture sit alongside sculptural objects and readymade-adjacent gestures, with wall texts drawn from essays, interviews and criticism written about the gallery's shows over the past decade and a half. It's less a survey than a scrapbook — a chance to see how a small, photography-attentive gallery's eye has developed across very different bodies of work, from Guidi's quiet Italian landscapes to Wyn Evans's conceptual gestures and Alison Wilding's sculpture.

For visitors unfamiliar with Large Glass, this is an efficient introduction to the gallery's range; for regulars, it works as a kind of anniversary album, with plenty of loans back from past exhibitions rehung in new company.

shows.title: Calligraphic Forms
shows.description:
Now in his seventh decade of practice, Sudanese modernist Ibrahim El-Salahi has spent much of his career worrying at a single question: how does a written mark become an image, a figure, a form? This focused exhibition traces that thread through calligraphic works spanning the 1980s to the 2010s, anchored by the extraordinary nine-panel Calligraphic Forms III / Alphabet 3 (1989) — a work El-Salahi has described as summing up his experimentation with Arabic calligraphy, freeing script characters back into their "original form: human, animal, plant, sound, cosmic shapes."

That piece connects to a lineage stretching back to Alphabet No. 1 (1960, now in the Princeton University Art Museum) and Alphabet No. 2 (1968, in the Met's collection), with the gallery's presentation effectively completing a decades-long conversation the artist has had with his own earlier work. Surrounding it are ink drawings, the artist's late Pain Relief works on paper, and paintings including Woman with Batoula Mask and The Tree, showing how the calligraphic impulse threads through even his more figurative and botanical subjects.

El-Salahi, sometimes called the "father of African modernism," was the first artist of African birth to receive a Tate Modern retrospective (2013); this tightly curated show is a good primer on the specific formal obsession — the transformation of Arabic script into pictorial form — that anchors his much broader body of work.

shows.title: REPRISE
shows.description:
George Rouy has spent the last several years pushing the human figure toward abstraction, and REPRISE reads as a kind of victory lap through that project — a return, as the title suggests, to motifs and gestures he has worked and reworked since breaking out in the London scene in the late 2010s. The paintings on view show bodies dissolving into and reforming out of one another: torsos twist into ribbons of colour, limbs blur into landscape, and faces flatten into something closer to smoke than to portraiture.

What makes Rouy's work distinct is how bodily the paint handling feels even as the imagery drifts toward the abstract — thin washes of acid greens and bruised purples pool and bleed the way skin might under pressure. The show's title gestures at repetition and return, and there's a real sense here of an artist revisiting his own vocabulary at a larger scale and with more confidence, rather than chasing novelty.

Rouy has become one of the more closely watched painters of his generation in Britain, and this show — running the length of the summer at the Peckham gallery that has represented him since early in his career — is a chance to see that development close up, away from the fair booths and secondary-market noise that now surround his work.

shows.title: Zana Masombuka / Spotlight: Benji Reid
shows.description:
October Gallery splits its two spaces between two very different photographers this autumn. In the main gallery, South African artist Zana Masombuka shows work drawn from several bodies of photography rooted in her Ndebele heritage — staged portraits built around beadwork, costume and ritual that read as much as performance documentation as fashion image. Across series like Nges'rhodlweni and Ubonani, she uses the camera to think through identity, ancestral memory and what it means to carry tradition into a hyper-contemporary register.

In the gallery's second space, a Spotlight presentation gathers photographs by Benji Reid, the British-Ghanaian photographer and former dancer/choreographer who built his practice on "hip-hop theatre" before turning it into elaborate staged self-portraiture. Reid's images place his own body in gravity-defying poses amid surreal props and sets, using that physical vocabulary to talk about fatherhood, mental health and life as an outsider. The two practices share a theatrical, staged approach to portraiture even as they draw on very different cultural reference points, and seeing them side by side makes for a sharp, well-paired two-hander.

Both artists work at the intersection of studio craft and personal narrative, and the pairing plays to October Gallery's long-running interest in contemporary art from Africa and its diaspora.

shows.title: The Black Paintings
shows.description:
James Lomax fills Sid Motion Gallery with fourteen windows cast in raw, unpigmented concrete, a number that deliberately echoes Goya's fourteen "Black Paintings" murals. Where Goya used pigment on plaster to register his late-life disillusionment, Lomax casts the same charge into a resolutely hard, grey material: each window is a fixed, fossilised fragment of a view that never fully resolves into a landscape.

The work turns on a familiar architectural device made strange. A window should orient you, telling you the time of day or the weather outside, but here each pane offers only a sliver of obscured information, denying the easy comfort of a clear outlook. Lomax layers in a second, more political register too, nodding to the "Overton Window" of acceptable public discourse — so the cast frames become as much about the limits of what can be said or seen as about domestic space itself.

Cast in a material associated with permanence, infrastructure and control, these sculptures sit somewhere between monument and barrier. The effect across the installation is quietly unsettling: rows of unyielding, identical apertures that trap the viewer's gaze inside the room rather than inviting it outward, turning a show about looking out into one about being held in place.

Lomax, a Royal Academy Schools graduate now in the Government Art Collection, has spent recent years working inside institutional and carceral spaces, including a residency at HMP Grendon, and that experience of enclosure and psychological structure clearly informs this body of work.

shows.title: Ridley: 2010–2020
shows.description:
This exhibition is the first in a planned series marking twenty-five years of Tim & Barry's work documenting underground music culture, and it centers on the decade the duo spent based at Ridley Road Studios in Hackney — the room that produced Just Jam, No Miming, The Lift and a run of now-legendary blue-screen live broadcasts featuring Skepta, Jammer, Novelist, DJ Rashad, SOPHIE, Loefah and Omar Souleyman among many others.

Rather than a conventional retrospective of finished artworks, the show translates a body of work made primarily for live broadcast and disappearance into physical objects: two tabletops from the studio itself, signed over a decade by everyone who passed through, alongside a showreel and a full list of collaborators. It's less about nostalgia than about making an argument — that grime, footwork, UK funky and the rest of the sounds that moved through that room were inseparable from the room itself, a cheap, precarious, since-gentrified space that no longer exists in the form that made the work possible.

Bringing the show to Harlesden, rather than restaging it in Hackney, is a deliberate move: this stretch of Brent has its own overlapping history of Caribbean sound-system culture and carnival, and shares the same pressures — rising rents, disappearing venues — that eventually closed the original studio. It's a smart, specific piece of music-culture history for anyone who lived through that era of internet-native live broadcasting, or wants to understand where a lot of contemporary UK sound came from.
shows.reception: Preview 26 July 2026, 6-9pm; Notting Hill Carnival Afters 30 August 2026, 7-10pm

shows.title: The Hospitable Threshold: 25 Years of Angel Mews
shows.description:
This is a valedictory show: Cubitt has just learned its lease at Angel Mews will not be renewed past October 2026, ending a twenty-five-year run in the same Islington space, and this exhibition — the last to be staged there — turns that fact into its subject. One half of the gallery holds material pulled from Cubitt's own archive, selected by curator Jennifer Irving with staff, tracing the artists, curators and communities who have passed through the building since the artist-run cooperative opened it in the early 2000s.

The other half belongs to Anne Tallentire, who has produced a new version of her long-running drawing series Setting Out, in which the floor plans of buildings are transposed directly onto gallery architecture using neon builder's line, screws and paper tags. Here Tallentire maps the entirety of the Angel Mews site — public galleries, offices, and the 32 artist studios alike — turning the whole building's footprint into a single spare, diagrammatic drawing. It's a fitting note for a space closing this chapter of its history: modest materials used to measure exactly what is about to be lost.

shows.title: Of Walking on Fire
shows.description:
Nhu Xuan Hua's first UK solo show turns her family's archive into strange, staged tableaux. Hua, a French photographer of Vietnamese heritage who has built a career shooting for Dior and Vogue, uses that same fashion-photography fluency here for a much more personal project: reworking old snapshots from her parents' flight from Vietnam and early years in France into dreamlike, uncanny compositions where figures blur and merge into one another.

The show is built around a specific silence — Hua's father is oral-deaf and communicates in spoken Vietnamese and self-taught French Sign Language, and no single language was shared across the household growing up. That gap between generations, and the impossibility of fully transmitting a family history through words alone, is the show's real subject. Gallery 1 sits with the loss and ambiguity of that inheritance; Gallery 2 turns toward repair, tracing a lineage of maternal figures through the lens of Đạo Mẫu, Vietnamese Mother Goddess worship, and includes a new commissioned work, Little Super in Versailles.

Photographs are staged alongside shelved trinkets and vases that nod to the visual language of Vietnamese temples, so the installation itself does some of the storytelling. It's a quiet, formally inventive show about what gets lost, and what gets carried forward, across a diaspora and a generation gap.

shows.title: Euphoria
shows.artist: Andreas Gursky, Emma Hart, Athen Kardashian & Nina Mhach Durban, Tarek Lakhrissi, Louis Morlæ
shows.description:
Bold Tendencies turns twenty this year, and it marks the anniversary with Euphoria, a rooftop season of five new site-specific commissions plus a parallel programme of orchestral, choral and dance performances staged across the car park's open-air levels. The visual art strand ranges wildly in scale and tone: Andreas Gursky shows the UK premiere of Cocoon II, a monumental aerial photograph of ravers inside Frankfurt's legendary Cocoon nightclub, while Emma Hart has built Last Chance Saloon, a full working bar rendered in raw, exuberant stoneware ceramics that visitors can actually stand inside.

Elsewhere the commissions turn more personal and speculative. Athen Kardashian & Nina Mhach Durban's shopfront sculpture collages the material culture of South London high streets — nail charms, hand-written postcards, faded shop signs — into a shrine to the neighbourhoods that shaped them, with an ongoing invitation for visitors to add their own votive locks. Tarek Lakhrissi's Rêverie is a colossal, chrysalis-like concrete and steel form lying prone on the rooftop, a meditation on withdrawal and transformation made under the shadow of rising political instability. Louis Morlæ contributes Euphoria Rover, a solar- and wind-powered robotic sculpture with its own AI-generated soundscape that periodically trundles across the roof like a lost, lovable machine.

Taken together the commissions read as a loose argument about where collective release still happens now — in a rave photograph, a pub, a chrysalis, a machine — at a moment the curators describe as one of "pathologised" intensity and algorithmic culture. It's an unusually ambitious use of the Peckham car park's improbable rooftop, and a fitting scale of ambition for an organisation marking two decades of turning a disused multi-storey into one of London's most-loved summer art destinations.

shows.title: Archaeology of Memory
shows.description:
Gabriel Chaile works in adobe, the sun-dried mud-and-straw material used across his native north-west Argentina for centuries, building it into monumental figures that read as part oven, part ancestor, part vessel. For his first major London institutional show, the Tucumán-born, Lisbon-based artist has filled Whitechapel Gallery with a new commission of these hulking anthropomorphic sculptures, each one doubling as a container for objects gathered from the neighborhood around the gallery.

That scavenging is central to the project. Chaile spent time collecting ceramics, tools, and other found or donated items from the streets and shops of Whitechapel and Spitalfields, and those objects now sit inside and around the adobe figures like offerings inside a shrine, or artifacts inside a dig. The effect is somewhere between an excavation site and a family altar - a set of guardians holding onto fragments of the East End's own layered, migrant history and setting it alongside the indigenous forms and craft traditions Chaile has spent his career reviving.

Chaile calls this method a "genealogy of form": the idea that a shape - a rounded belly, a hollow mouth, a squat stance - keeps resurfacing across centuries and cultures, picking up new meaning each time it reappears. His figures are unmistakably bodies, but they're also furnaces, urns, and totems, and the installation as a whole asks visitors to move through it the way an archaeologist might move through a site, piecing together a story from what's been kept and what's been found.

The show follows Chaile's shortlisting for the Fourth Plinth commission and his presentation at Studio Voltaire, and it's a rare chance to see his large-scale sculpture on this scale in London. Photographs from the installation show a room dense with these earthen figures - raw, tactile, and quietly monumental - making it one of the more physically striking gallery shows on in the city this summer.

shows.title: Picture Making
shows.description:
Cecily Brown made her name in 1990s New York with paintings that pushed figuration to the edge of abstraction - bodies, fruit, and animals dissolving into thick, urgent brushwork. This show, staged a few hundred feet from where she played as a child, is billed as a homecoming: her first major solo presentation of paintings in a UK institution since 2005, after three decades based in New York.

The exhibition leans into Brown's long fascination with English park life and woodland scenes, themes that take on particular resonance given the gallery's setting inside Kensington Gardens. New paintings made specifically for the show hang alongside key works dating back to 2001, plus a run of recent monotypes and drawings, so visitors get a sense of how her recurring motifs - amorous couples, tangled undergrowth, half-glimpsed creatures - have mutated over twenty-odd years without ever quite resolving into calm.

There's a darker undertow running through the new work too, drawn from Brown's memories of children's book illustration and the more unsettling register of cautionary tales - fairy-tale menace pushed up against loose, painterly bravado. It's a chance to see a major British painter's return to form on a scale rarely offered outside a museum survey, in galleries that suit her large, immersive canvases well.

shows.title: Staging Resistance: Tessa Boffin, Rotimi Fani-Kayode and Sunil Gupta in 1980s London
shows.artist: Tessa Boffin, Rotimi Fani-Kayode, Sunil Gupta
shows.description:
Three photographers who moved in the same tight, radical circle of 1980s London queer culture are brought together here, each represented by the body of work that made their reputation. Sunil Gupta's "Pretended" Family Relationships pairs staged portraits of same-sex couples with documentary shots of anti-Section 28 protests, using the wording of that homophobic law against itself. Rotimi Fani-Kayode's Bodies of Experience turns the studio into a ritual space, framing the Black male body through Yoruba spirituality and dramatic chiaroscuro. Tessa Boffin's Angelic Rebels: Lesbians and Safer Sex reimagines the angel as an openly sexual lesbian figure, mixing safer-sex instruction with theatrical fantasy.

What makes the grouping more than a survey is the real history behind it: Gupta and Boffin met in London in 1988 and went on to co-organise the landmark show Ecstatic Antibodies, which also included Fani-Kayode's work shortly after his death from AIDS-related illness in 1989. Seeing the three practices side by side reconstructs a specific, embattled moment - the AIDS crisis and Section 28 - when photography itself became an act of political self-definition.

The show arrives alongside a wave of institutional attention for all three artists, including Gupta's career retrospective at Kettle's Yard and Fani-Kayode's inclusion in the Barbican's Project a Black Planet, so it's a timely chance to see the more intimate, gallery-scaled originals that sit behind those bigger surveys.

shows.title: David and Yuko Juda Art Foundation Award
shows.description:
Now in its seventh edition, the David and Yuko Juda Art Foundation Award gives a single artist £50,000 with no strings attached, selected by a shortlist that changes curator every year. For 2026 the honor of choosing goes to art historian Alyce Mahon, and her seven nominees — Laia Abril, Aziza Kadyri, Amak Mahmoodian, Niamh O'Malley, Ro Robertson, Soheila Sokhanvari and Olivia Sterling — each get a work or small group of works on view, making the show a genuine survey of very different practices rather than a single curatorial thesis.

The range on view is wide: Abril's research-driven photographic project on endometriosis sits alongside Kadyri's hand-embroidered textile elegy for the vanished Aral Sea, Mahmoodian's dream-based installation drawing on collaborators from fourteen countries, O'Malley's poised sculptures incorporating salvaged architectural glass, Robertson's steel-and-drawing installation rooted in the Cornish landscape, Sokhanvari's jewel-like egg-tempera portraits on vellum, and Sterling's brightly colored, sharply satirical paintings of British domestic life. The winner is announced at the opening reception.

This marks the first time the Foundation's exhibition is held at Annely Juda's new Hanover Square townhouse, and it's a useful snapshot of some of the sharper, more research-minded corners of contemporary British and UK-based practice — recommended for anyone who wants a fast survey of names likely to be talked about over the next few years.

shows.title: Robert Dukes: New Paintings
shows.description:
Robert Dukes' first solo show in six years, and his debut with Bernard Jacobson Gallery, is built almost entirely from still life — jugs, quinces, pears, a wine glass, a child's toy duck — painted in oil on board with the patient, analytical eye of a painter trained under Euan Uglow and Patrick George at the Slade. Dukes isn't after a single focal object; he's after what he calls an "analogy of forms," matching colour and shadow across unrelated things so a beer bottle, a quince and the negative space between them all carry equal weight in the composition.

What distinguishes this body of work from Dukes' earlier still lifes is a willingness to let objects run off the edge of the canvas — a mug, a bowl, a plate's shadow cropped at the frame, as in Pears on Purple — so the paintings read less like arranged tableaux and more like fragments of an actual room glimpsed in passing. Some objects are loaded with private meaning (a wooden duck that belonged to his late uncle), others are studio ephemera (empty paint boxes, a Posca pen), but Dukes treats them all with the same unhurried, observational attention, working from life rather than photographs.

The show arrives with a catalogue featuring an essay by critic Andrew Lambirth, underlining how seriously Dukes' quiet, classically grounded painting is regarded within the current British figurative scene — a good chance to see an artist who has spent years refining a single, exacting mode of looking.

shows.title: A hard line to bend
shows.description:
This is the first exhibition at a major UK institution for Liz Larner, one of the most respected American sculptors of the post-minimal generation, and it gathers roughly a decade of her work around a loose but pointed theme: the transformation of matter, from geologic time to the plastics we throw away tomorrow. The show moves through a series of rooms rather than presenting a single thesis statement, tracking Larner's restless movement between materials — clay, bronze, plastic, wood — and the very different registers of meaning each one carries.

The anchor of the exhibition is Larner's wall-mounted ceramic tablets, fired and glazed objects that sit somewhere between painting and sculpture, their cracked and polychrome surfaces the visible record of the making process itself. Nearby, assemblages built from discarded single-use plastic are placed in dialogue with a series of ceramic "asteroids" named for female figures from myth, a pairing that yokes contemporary waste to ancient cosmology and quietly argues that even inert matter carries some kind of charge or history. The exhibition's title work, a new bronze-and-branch sculpture referencing Lilith — the Mesopotamian and Jewish folkloric figure who has become shorthand for female autonomy — anchors the show's eco-feminist and post-humanist undercurrents.

Larner has spent three decades treating sculpture as a way of testing how bodies and objects share space, and this show, drawing on a major 2022 survey at the Walker Art Center and SculptureCenter, gives London a rare chance to see that thinking at scale. It's a strong opening to the gallery's autumn season and one of the more ambitious sculpture surveys on view in the city this year.

shows.title: Salvation
shows.description:
Peter Howson's new body of work retells the life of Christ across a sequence of interconnected oil paintings on gesso panel, continuing the devotional, expressionist vein that has run through the Glasgow painter's practice since his own well-documented religious conversion in the 1990s. Howson made his name as one of the "New Glasgow Boys," painting brutal, muscular scenes of urban Glasgow and later the Bosnian war as an official war artist; here that same physical intensity is turned toward Gospel narrative.

The gesso-panel technique gives the paintings a matte, almost fresco-like surface, and the interconnected format suggests Howson is building toward something closer to a modern Stations of the Cross than a set of discrete pictures. Given his history of turning personal crisis into scripture-adjacent imagery, this reads as one of his most direct statements of faith to date, and a useful counterpoint to the more secular abstraction on view elsewhere at the gallery this autumn.

shows.title: Anish Kapoor
shows.description:
Thirty years after his first major UK survey at this same address, Anish Kapoor returns to the Hayward with a show that fills the entire brutalist building. It's a career-spanning look at the strategies he's built a reputation on: mirror-polished steel forms that warp and swallow the viewer's reflection, voids that seem to open straight through the gallery floor, and objects coated in Vantablack, the light-devouring pigment Kapoor has used almost as a signature material for the past decade.

Alongside the illusionistic sculpture, the exhibition brings in newer, messier work — paintings and sculptures dealing frankly with blood, viscera and the body's fragility, a rawer register than the polished spectacle Kapoor is best known for. There are also new installations in his recurring red, pieces that continue his interest in turning architecture and interior space inside out.

Curated by outgoing Hayward director Ralph Rugoff as his final show after two decades leading the gallery, this is being pitched as one of the major London exhibitions of the year, and it's easy to see why: few artists command a building-sized survey with this much visual force, oscillating between wonder and unease.

shows.title: A Life of Navigation
shows.description:
Tucked into the Hayward's free HENI Project Space, this compact show gathers four works by Taiwanese artist Musquiqui Chihying, whose deadpan, prop-heavy videos treat the absurdities of contemporary urban life as material for both comedy and critique. Two earlier pieces, The Jog and The Toyota, sit alongside two new video installations that turn a sly eye on artificial intelligence, gaming culture, and the friction between manual labour and automation.

The inflatable teal car that anchors one gallery — deflating and reflating, seemingly mid-collapse on a curbside parking space — is a good index of the show's tone: playful on the surface, but pointed underneath, using humour and low-tech spectacle to needle at the colonial undercurrents of the tech industry's promises of progress.

It's a small, free-to-visit show rather than a survey, but for an artist working across installation, video, photography and sculpture with this much wit, it's a worthwhile detour on a visit built around the Kapoor blockbuster upstairs.
