shows.title: Atlantic Ridge Multiplicity
shows.description:
Teresa Solar Abboud's first UK solo show brings her hand-worked clay sculptures, works on paper and video together around a recurring idea: the world as a series of hybrid, half-legible bodies caught mid-transformation. Her best-known works, the Tunnel Boring Machines shown at the 2022 Venice Biennale's Milk of Dreams, paired visibly hand-thrown clay with glossy resin appendages resembling flippers or beaks — speculative creatures standing in for the hidden forces that shape the ground beneath a city.

The new pieces here extend that same logic of interrelation and metamorphosis into new territory, moving between subterranean landscapes, ecological entanglement and the subatomic, always with that same tension between rough, handmade clay surfaces and bright, precisely finished synthetic elements. It's a practice that treats geology and biology as versions of the same problem — how matter organizes itself into bodies, tunnels, and systems that only partly make sense to us.

The show follows Solar Abboud's outdoor Hayward Gallery installation Mother Tongue and a run of European solo exhibitions in 2025, and marks a strong London debut for an artist whose sculptural language is genuinely hard to place alongside anyone else's.

shows.description:
Serpentine's Education Space has been turned over this summer to an open archive documenting the institution's decade-plus of work at the intersection of art and emerging technology — blockchain, AI, game engines and the rest. It's less a conventional exhibition than a hybrid reading room, listening space and research archive, pulling together audio recordings, publications, photographs and material from past digital commissions produced by Serpentine's Arts Technologies department.

The display is deliberately unfinished: framed as "an active archive," it keeps adding audience-contributed material for the duration of its run, including a set of specially commissioned receipt poems. It functions as an accessible way into work that can otherwise feel opaque or overly technical — a chance to see the paper trail and physical ephemera behind years of commissions most visitors only encountered as finished digital artworks.

It's a low-key, research-forward complement to Serpentine's higher-profile shows next door, worth a visit if you're interested in how an arts institution builds and preserves its own institutional memory around fast-moving technology.

shows.title: Weight of Matter
shows.description:
Monika Sosnowska takes over both of South London Gallery's buildings for the biggest UK museum-scale showing of her work in years, filling the Victorian Main Gallery and two floors of the Fire Station with sculptures built from steel, concrete and other hallmarks of modernist construction. The Polish artist is known for taking real architectural elements — staircases, window frames, structural beams — and subjecting them to violence: crushing, twisting, collapsing them until they read as ruins of buildings that may never have existed.

At the Main Gallery, a group of large-scale works, some weighing over half a tonne, hang from the rafters beneath the glass roof lantern like industrial carcasses, fusing into one another rather than resolving into separate objects. The Fire Station portion, housed in a converted Victorian fire station, is more site-responsive: a collapsed black staircase answers the building's own white metal stairs, a garden gallery is overrun with rebar "plants," and upstairs, in the former firemen's quarters, painted steel pieces suggest crumpled paper and peeling walls that echo the building's own history of decay and renovation.

Sosnowska's work has always carried a political charge, rooted in her memory of Poland's transition out of Communism and the wave of ambitious modernist building that came with it; here that history collides with the specific texture of a South London Victorian building. The show also marks the first UK display of her intricate paper maquettes, small studies rarely shown outside the studio, offering a rare look at how these monumental, violent-feeling sculptures actually begin.
